title: Float, dependencies & the network diagram
blurb: Read a network diagram, recognise dependencies and explain what float is and why it matters.
question: The kitchen fitter wants to start the wall tiling two days later than planned. The project manager agrees, saying 'tiling has two days of float'. What is float, and will this delay move the handover date?

teach.h: Dependencies: what has to come first
teach.body: A dependency is a link between activities: one cannot start (or finish) until another has reached a certain point. You can't plaster until the cables are in the walls; you can't fit units until they've been delivered. A network diagram draws this logic: each activity is a box (a node) and each arrow is a dependency. Follow the arrows and you see every path from start to finish.

Meaning
Example

teach.caption: Finish-to-start is by far the most common, and the one the exam expects you to recognise.

teach.caption: Illustration only: the PFQ never asks you to calculate float, just to know what it means.

teach.body: Float (also called slack) is the amount of time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project end date; strictly, this is total float. Plainly: it's breathing space. Activities on the critical path have zero float. Activities on shorter paths have float equal to the gap between their path and the critical path.

teach.h: Elm Road on a Gantt chart
teach.caption: The outlined tails are float. Tiling can start up to two days late and the handover on day 10 still holds.

teach.h: What happens as float is used up
Why the PM cares about float
teach.body: Float tells the project manager where the schedule can flex. Non-critical work can start later to suit people's availability, absorb small delays or be moved to even out resource peaks (resource smoothing). But float is finite: every day used is a day gone, and an activity that uses all its float becomes critical. Good PMs track float being consumed, not just activities finishing.

rows.label: Created by
values: The sponsor or PM setting it aside

teach.text: Float is NOT padding added to an estimate and NOT a reserve the sponsor holds. It simply exists because some paths are shorter than the critical path. Also remember: zero float means critical, and a finish-to-start link means the next activity can't START until the previous one FINISHES.

items: Dependencies link activities; finish-to-start is the most common.
A network diagram shows activities as boxes and dependencies as arrows.
Float (slack): how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the end date.
Critical activities have zero float; using up all its float makes an activity critical.
Float shows where the schedule has flexibility; it is not a contingency reserve.

summary: You can now read a simple network diagram, recognise finish-to-start and other dependencies, and explain float as the time an activity can slip without delaying the project end date. You also know that using up float turns an activity critical, and that float is not contingency.

A.q: What is meant by 'float' in a project schedule?
options: Extra budget set aside to cover risk events
Time added to estimates as a safety margin
The gap between planned and actual dates
Time a task can slip without delaying the end
A.why: Float is the amount of time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project end date.

whyNot.0: Money set aside for risks is a contingency budget, not float.
whyNot.1: Padding estimates is a different (and poor) practice; float comes from the network logic.
whyNot.2: The gap between planned and actual is a schedule variance.

A.q: Which type of dependency is the most common in project network diagrams?
A.why: Finish-to-start, where the next activity begins once the previous one finishes, is by far the most common.

whyNot.0: Start-to-start is used where activities begin together, which is less common.
whyNot.2: Finish-to-finish is used where activities must end together, which is less common.
whyNot.3: Start-to-finish is the rarest type of dependency.

A.q: Complete the statement: in a finish-to-start dependency, the successor activity cannot ______ until its predecessor has finished.
A.why: Finish-to-start means the second activity can only start once the first has finished.

whyNot.1: A link controlling when the successor finishes would be finish-to-finish.
whyNot.2: Estimating can happen at any time; dependencies govern when work is done.
whyNot.3: Resources can be planned in advance; the dependency governs the start.

B.q: On the Elm Road kitchen, tiling has two days of float. The tiler starts one day late. What is the effect on the handover date?
B.why: The one-day delay is within tiling's two days of float, so the handover date doesn't move.

whyNot.0: The delay is absorbed by float, so the end date does not slip.
whyNot.1: Float means delay up to two days is absorbed, not added on.
whyNot.2: Starting late can never bring the handover forward.

B.q: What does a network diagram mainly show?
options: Who is accountable for each package
How the budget is split by account
B.why: A network diagram shows activities (nodes) and the dependencies (arrows) between them, revealing the paths and the critical path.

whyNot.0: Accountability is shown in a responsibility assignment matrix.
whyNot.2: Budget split by account is the cost breakdown structure.
whyNot.3: Stakeholder power is shown on a power/interest grid.

B.q: Which of the following is another term for float?
B.why: Float is also known as slack.

whyNot.0: Lag is a deliberate wait inserted between linked activities, such as drying time.
whyNot.1: A buffer is a deliberate time allowance, as used in critical chain, not the same as float.
whyNot.3: Contingency is a reserve set aside for risk, not float from the network logic.

C.q: A non-critical activity has used up all of its float. Which statement is now correct?
options: It can still slip a little
C.why: With zero float left, any further delay will delay the end date, so the activity is now critical.

whyNot.0: With no float left, any slip now delays the project end date.
whyNot.1: Re-estimating doesn't change the fact that it now has zero float.
whyNot.3: The work is still required; it has simply become time-critical.

C.q:
Which TWO statements about float are correct?
1. Critical activities have zero float
2. Float is set aside by the sponsor as a reserve
3. Float shows where the schedule is flexible
4. Float is added to every estimate for safety
C.why: Critical activities have zero float, and float reveals where the schedule has flexibility.

whyNot.0: Float is not a sponsor's reserve; that describes contingency.
whyNot.1: Neither statement is true: float comes from the network logic.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: float is not padding added to estimates.

C.q: Plastering cannot start until the first-fix electrics are complete. What does this describe?
C.why: One activity (plastering) can only start once another (first fix) has finished: a finish-to-start dependency.

whyNot.0: Start-to-start would mean plastering could begin when first fix begins.
whyNot.2: Over-allocation is demand above availability for a resource, not a logical link.
whyNot.3: A milestone marks an event; this describes a link between two activities.

reteach.title: Think of catching a train with time to spare
reteach.question: Your train leaves at 9:00 and the walk takes 20 minutes. You're ready at 8:30. How much can you dawdle?

blocks.body: You must leave by 8:40 to make the train. Being ready at 8:30 gives you 10 minutes of float: you can make a coffee and still catch it. Spend 10 minutes and your float is gone; the walk is now critical. Spend 15 and you miss the train. The walk can't start until you're ready: that's a finish-to-start dependency.
On a project, float is the same spare time, built into the network wherever a path is shorter than the critical path. It lets you absorb small delays or move work around, until it is used up.

explain.body: A network diagram shows each activity as a box and each dependency as an arrow. The most common link is finish-to-start: B starts when A finishes. Following the arrows reveals every path through the project.

test.q: In a network diagram, what do the arrows between the activities represent?
test.why: Arrows show the logical dependencies between activities.

whyNot.0: Costs are recorded in the budget and CBS.
whyNot.2: Risks are recorded in the risk register.
whyNot.3: Resources are assigned to activities, not drawn as arrows.

explain.body: Float (slack) is the time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project end date. It exists on paths that are shorter than the critical path.

test.q: An activity with float can be delayed by up to that amount without delaying which of these?
test.why: Total float is measured against the project end date.

whyNot.0: Float is not defined against a gate review.
whyNot.1: Sponsor sign-off isn't the reference point for float.
whyNot.3: Invoicing has nothing to do with float.

explain.body: Float is consumed as an activity starts late or runs long. When it reaches zero the activity is critical; any further delay pushes out the end date. That's why PMs watch float being used, not only finish dates.

test.q: Why should a project manager track how much float has been used, not just whether tasks finish?
options: Float must be repaid to the sponsor
Float shows the cost of each task
Float decides who does each task
test.why: As float runs out, a non-critical activity becomes critical and starts to threaten the end date.

whyNot.1: Float isn't a loan from the sponsor; it comes from the network.
whyNot.3: Who does the work is shown in the RAM, not by float.

explain.body: Contingency is a deliberate reserve held for risks. Float isn't set aside by anyone: it simply exists because some paths through the network are shorter than the critical path.

options: A time reserve the sponsor holds
Paths shorter than the critical one
test.why: Float exists wherever a path through the network is shorter than the critical path.

whyNot.0: A reserve held for risk is contingency, not float.
whyNot.1: Padding estimates hides risk; it isn't how float arises.
whyNot.2: Budget is money, while float is time.
